comments.body:
I found a working configuration workaround on my machine. No driver changes were required.

**Original setup:** Ethernet uplink, AmneziaWG, Brave excluded by application, site-based split tunneling disabled. Enabling Windows Mobile Hotspot broke connectivity in Brave.

### What worked

1. Changed Windows Internet Connection Sharing to share the **AmneziaVPN adapter** with the Wi-Fi Direct hotspot adapter, instead of sharing Ethernet.
2. After this change, Brave could connect directly through Ethernet, but the phone initially had no Internet access.
3. Added an on-link host route for the phone’s static address (`192.168.137.201/32`) through the hotspot adapter.

The route needed special handling: Amnezia’s `WindowsRouteMonitor` also cloned the initial host route into the VPN interface, causing return traffic to the phone to take the wrong interface.

Setting the hotspot host route’s metric to `0x5e72` (24178), the existing `EXCLUSION_ROUTE_METRIC` value recognized by the route monitor, prevented that route from being cloned. I also removed the VPN `/32` clone created during testing.

A small local helper now maintains this single host route and starts at Windows sign-in.

### Verified

- Excluded Brave connects directly through Ethernet.
- Ordinary VPN traffic continues through the VPN.
- The phone has Internet access through the shared VPN, with cellular data disabled.
- Both Brave and the phone still work after reconnecting the VPN and after toggling Mobile Hotspot.

A full Windows reboot has not yet been tested.

### Limitations

This is a **workaround**, not a fix for the original driver/ICS interaction. It depends on an internal route-metric marker and the phone’s fixed IP address, so it should not be treated as a general solution.

It also changes the phone’s Internet path: the phone now uses the shared VPN.

comments.issue_title: Linux: IPv6 endpoint not bracketed before wireguard-go IPC, peer creation fails with IPC error -22
comments.body:
Reproduced on AmneziaVPN **5.1.0.6** (Linux Mint 22.3, userspace `amneziawg-go`, kernel has no AmneziaWG module) with an **IPv6-only** endpoint: the host name has an AAAA record and **no A record at all**, so there is no IPv4 fallback path. Same symptom as reported here, plus a second defect that blocks the connection even after this one is fixed.

## 1. The endpoint is handed to wireguard-go without brackets (this issue)

```
[DEBUG] WireguardUtilsLinux : Configuring peer <key> via 2001:db8:1234:5678::
[DEBUG] WireguardGo : ERROR: (amn0) IPC error -22: failed to set endpoint 2001:db8:1234:5678:::443:
        invalid ip:port "2001:db8:1234:5678:::443", IPv6 addresses must be surrounded by square brackets
[ERROR] DaemonLocalServerConnection : Failed to activate the interface
```

The literal travels through the **IPv4** branch of `client/platforms/linux/daemon/wireguardutilslinux.cpp` (`updatePeer()`), so the branch that adds brackets never runs:

```cpp
if (!config.m_serverIpv4AddrIn.isNull()) {
    out << "endpoint=" << config.m_serverIpv4AddrIn << ":";      // ← takes the IPv6 literal, no brackets
} else if (!config.m_serverIpv6AddrIn.isNull()) {
    out << "endpoint=[" << config.m_serverIpv6AddrIn << "]:";
}
out << config.m_serverPort << "\n";
```

`m_serverIpv4AddrIn` is filled from `serverIpv4AddrIn` in `client/daemon/daemon.cpp`, which is where the resolved address ends up regardless of its family. `client/daemon/interfaceconfig.cpp` (`toWgConf`) has the same shape, with the IPv6 `Endpoint` line commented out. The error text itself comes from Go's `net/netip` (`netip.ParseAddrPort`, called from `amneziawg-go`'s `conn.StdNetBind.ParseEndpoint`), which deliberately refuses to guess where the address ends and the port begins.

Minimal fix that needs no guessing — bracket by content, in the same `if`:

```cpp
const QString addr = config.m_serverIpv4AddrIn;
out << "endpoint=" << (addr.contains(':') ? "[" + addr + "]" : addr) << ":";
```

(or keep the families apart where the config is populated, then the existing IPv6 branch works as written).

## 2. Separate defect: no exclusion route is created for an IPv6 endpoint

With (1) fixed the peer is created, routes are installed — and the handshake still cannot complete, because the endpoint ends up inside the tunnel:

```
[DEBUG] LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for 2001:db8:1234:5678::/128
[WARNING] LinuxRouteMonitor : No default gateway available, skipping exclusion route
[DEBUG] LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding route to ::/1
[DEBUG] LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding route to 8000::/1
[DEBUG] Daemon : Checking for handshake...
[DEBUG] DaemonLocalServerConnection : Command received: deactivate        # ~13 s later, no handshake
```

`::/1` + `8000::/1` cover the endpoint as well, so the handshake packets are sent into the tunnel that is still down. On the same host the IPv4 default gateway exists and IPv4 exclusions work (we keep a `/32` route for the server address), so this looks like an IPv6 gap in the gateway lookup, not a missing route. Adding `2001:db8:1234:5678::/128 via <current IPv6 default gateway> dev <iface>` by hand makes the handshake go through immediately.

## Workaround we run meanwhile

Patched `amneziawg-go`'s `conn.StdNetBind.ParseEndpoint` to also accept a bare `addr:port` form (port separated by the last colon, remainder must parse as an IPv6 address) — that removes the `IPC error -22` — plus the manual `/128` exclusion route. With those two the tunnel comes up and carries traffic. Both fixes are on our side only; the report is about the client.

Full logs (`-u AmneziaVPN.service`) available on request.

comments.issue_title: Linux 5.0.1.5: exclusion routes never installed — netlink route dump overflows the   fixed 8 KiB buffer
comments.body:
Today I have met this issue too, trying to install huge list of sites (> 9k) to exclude from vpn.
Two things not covered above, both specific to "All sites except listed" split tunneling. Reproduced on 5.1.0.6.

### 1. A long site list overflows the buffer by itself, and both open PRs only move the cutoff.
`rtmSendRoute()` calls `getGatewayAndIface()` once per exclusion route, and every route it installs adds 60 bytes to the next dump. So the list fills the buffer partway through the connect, even on a host with a small routing table. 

| Receive buffer | Exclusions installed |
|---|---|
| 8 KiB (current) | 115 |
| 64 KiB (size used in #3231) | 1,071 |
| 128 KiB (size used in #3170) | 2,163 |
| Parse each datagram, stop at the default route | all installed |

So a fix needs either a parser that never accumulates the whole dump, or the gateway resolved once per `activate()`/`switchServer()` and passed down.

### 2. Disconnect can't remove the routes.
`deleteExclusionRoute()` takes the same `RTN_THROW` branch, so it does the same lookup. At disconnect the table is still over the limit, so every delete is skipped and all installed exclusions stay in the main table (in the netns test, 0 of 115 were removed). The next connect then can't add any exclusion, the endpoint route included. Deleting shouldn't need the lookup at all: the kernel deletes the route by prefix without a gateway.

comments.issue_title: [Windows 11 26H2] Built-in AmneziaWG fails with WSAEFAULT, while standalone AmneziaWG 3.1.0 works
comments.body:
# Windows 11: VPN clients hang on connecting due to incorrect routing of VPN server endpoints through the TUN interface

## Environment

- Windows 11 Home, version 26H2 (OS build 26300.9818).
- Android phone used for USB tethering.
- USB network adapter: Samsung Mobile USB Remote NDIS (RNDIS).
- VPN clients tested: AmneziaWG / AmneziaVPN and HAPP (Xray core).
- The same VPN configurations worked on Android using the same network connection.

## Symptoms

VPN clients on Windows started normally but could not establish a working connection.

Observed behavior:

- AmneziaWG remained stuck at the connecting stage.
- HAPP started its Xray core and created its local SOCKS5 proxy, but requests through the proxy timed out.
- HAPP's TUN interface was created successfully, but traffic did not pass through it.
- The same HAPP configuration worked on an Android phone connected to the same Wi-Fi network.
- Reinstalling VPN clients, rebooting Windows, resetting routes and Winsock did not solve the problem.
- Disabling the Kaspersky NDIS network filter did not change anything.

## Diagnosis

The issue was related to Windows routing when a VPN TUN interface was active.

When HAPP started, it created a virtual network interface and installed a default route (`0.0.0.0/0`) through that interface.

As a result, Windows could also select the VPN tunnel as the route for packets addressed to the VPN server itself.

This creates a routing/bootstrap loop: the VPN client needs to reach its remote server through the physical network interface before the tunnel can work, but Windows may attempt to send that connection through the tunnel being established.

The issue was identified using PowerShell:

```powershell
Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress <VPN_SERVER_IP> |
Format-List InterfaceAlias, InterfaceIndex, DestinationPrefix, NextHop
```

When the result showed the virtual VPN interface instead of the physical network adapter, it indicated incorrect route selection.

## Workaround: Add an explicit host route for each VPN server

The solution was to add a `/32` host route for each VPN server endpoint, forcing Windows to reach that endpoint directly through the physical network interface.

### 1. Identify the physical network interface and gateway

For Android USB tethering:

```powershell
Get-NetIPConfiguration |
Where-Object {$_.IPv4DefaultGateway} |
Format-Table InterfaceAlias, InterfaceIndex,
@{N='IP';E={$_.IPv4Address.IPAddress -join ','}},
@{N='Gateway';E={$_.IPv4DefaultGateway.NextHop -join ','}} -AutoSize
```

Important: use the actual gateway address, not the computer's own IP address.

### 2. Add a route for the VPN server

Run PowerShell as Administrator:

```powershell
New-NetRoute `
-DestinationPrefix "<VPN_SERVER_IP>/32" `
-InterfaceIndex <PHYSICAL_INTERFACE_INDEX> `
-NextHop "<PHYSICAL_GATEWAY_IP>" `
-RouteMetric 1 `
-PolicyStore ActiveStore
```

For example, use the interface index and gateway belonging to the currently active Wi-Fi or USB RNDIS connection.

### 3. Verify the route

```powershell
Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress <VPN_SERVER_IP> |
Format-List InterfaceAlias, InterfaceIndex, DestinationPrefix, NextHop
```

The result should point to the physical network adapter (Wi-Fi or USB RNDIS), NOT the VPN TUN interface.

### 4. Repeat for other VPN endpoints

Each VPN client may connect to a different server IP.

In my case:
- Adding a host route for the HAPP/Xray server through the physical Wi-Fi gateway restored HAPP connectivity.
- Adding a separate host route for the AmneziaWG server through the Android USB RNDIS gateway restored AmneziaWG connectivity.

The routes must use the gateway and interface of the currently active physical connection.

## Important notes

- Do not use the computer's own interface IP as `NextHop`. Use `IPv4DefaultGateway.NextHop`.
- Do not assume that all VPN clients use the same server IP.
- HAPP may use automatic server selection or multiple remote endpoints. Check the actual remote IP addresses used by Xray.

I have the same issue on Ubuntu 24.04 with AmneziaWG.

### System info

- **OS:** Ubuntu 24.04
- **AmneziaVPN:** 5.0.3.0 (Sep 18, 2026, `de93650`)
- **systemd-resolved:** 255.4-1ubuntu8.18
- **Protocol:** AmneziaWG
- **VPN interface:** `amn0`
- **Connection:** Imported using an encrypted key

### What happens

- VPN connects successfully, but websites don't load.
- Pinging IP addresses works, but DNS requests fail.
- `resolvectl` commands hang when the VPN is connected.
- `systemd-resolved` starts using almost 100% CPU.
- The `amn0` interface has no DNS servers assigned (`Current Scopes: none`).
- Everything works normally after disconnecting the VPN.

One thing I noticed is that AmneziaVPN shows `1.1.1.1` and `1.0.0.1` as DNS servers, but the `.conf` file provided by my VPN service for the same server contains `8.8.4.4` and a custom DNS server used by the provider.

I tested both DNS servers from that config, and they work correctly through the VPN. Requests to `1.1.1.1` and `8.8.8.8` fail.

### Workaround

I made a small systemd service that checks whether the `amn0` interface exists.

When the VPN connects, it temporarily replaces `/etc/resolv.conf` with the DNS servers from the provider's `.conf` file (`8.8.4.4` and the provider's custom DNS server).

When the VPN disconnects, it restores the original symlink:

`/etc/resolv.conf -> ../run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf`

After this, websites load normally, and `systemd-resolved` CPU usage eventually drops to 0%.

The service also works after reconnecting the VPN, so I don't need to change DNS settings manually every time.

issues.title: feat(acl): switch ACL engine to expr
issues.body:
Replaces the ACL engine with one based on [expr](https://expr-lang.org/), so rules can match on more than the destination. The main use case is routing by authentication ID:

```yaml
acl:
  rules:
    - outbound: alice_exit
      match: auth.id == "alice"
    - outbound: reject
      match: geoip("cn") || cidr("10.0.0.0/8", client.ip)
    - outbound: default
      match: dst.port == 53 && cidr("8.8.8.8")
      hijack: 1.1.1.1
    - legacy: reject(geosite:category-ads-all)
    - legacyFile: /etc/hysteria/acl.txt
    - outbound: direct
```

- New `acl.rules` / `acl.rulesFile` (YAML list). Rules see `proto`, `dst.{host,port,ipv4,ipv6}`, `auth.id` and `client.{ip,port}`, plus `domain`, `suffix`, `cidr`, `geoip`, `geosite` and `legacy` matchers. Called with one argument they match the destination like before; with two, an explicit value (e.g. `client.ip`). Typos, non-boolean rules and unknown GeoIP/GeoSite names fail at load time
- Legacy `acl.file` / `acl.inline` keep working and are translated to expr internally. Legacy lines can also be mixed into `acl.rules` via `legacy` / `legacyFile` entries, so you can add a rule above an existing list without converting it
- `hysteria acl translate` prints the legacy rules as `acl.rules` YAML; `hysteria acl test -c server.yaml [--auth ID] [--client IP] [--proto udp] host:port` shows which rule and outbound a request would use, without connecting
- The match cache key only includes auth ID / client address when a rule uses them, so legacy rulesets cache exactly as before

**Breaking changes**
- `server.Outbound` methods now take a `*server.RequestInfo` (auth ID and client address) as the first argument. This affects programs that embed core
- Legacy port ranges starting at 0 (e.g. `udp/0-100`, `tcp/0`) used to match every port; they now match only the given range

**Performance** (100 rules, no GeoIP/GeoSite)

| | Old engine | New engine |
|---|---|---|
| Cache hit | 184 ns | 114 ns |
| Cache miss (no rule matches) | 2.9 µs | 8.4 µs |

Misses cost about 3× more because expr allocates an argument list per function call. A miss happens once per new destination (up to the 1024-entry cache), and is small next to the DNS lookup every request already does when ACL is enabled. Hits are faster because the cache key is now a struct instead of a formatted string.

**Testing**
- Every existing compile test runs against both the old compiler (kept in a test file for now) and the translated rules. A comparison test checks 30 legacy rule types against ~700 requests and requires identical results except the port-0 fix. A fuzzer found no mismatches in ~850k inputs
- Integration test checks the auth ID and client address reach the outbound for TCP, the first UDP packet, and later UDP destinations
- End to end with two users: the same destination is rejected for one and allowed for the other

comments.issue_title: Salamander and Masquerade
comments.body: Yes, they work together. With the v2.13.0 server and client, a config that has both `obfs: salamander` and `masquerade` (including `listenHTTP`/`listenHTTPS`) starts normally. A client with the right obfs password connects and passes traffic, and clients with no or a wrong obfs password time out. Obfs wraps the UDP socket before QUIC sees it ([server.go#L365](https://github.com/apernet/hysteria/blob/ca8fbd874fd6ca82413948de6dc5924405e103e1/app/cmd/server.go#L365), [#L433-L456](https://github.com/apernet/hysteria/blob/ca8fbd874fd6ca82413948de6dc5924405e103e1/app/cmd/server.go#L433-L456), [core/server/server.go#L67-L70](https://github.com/apernet/hysteria/blob/ca8fbd874fd6ca82413948de6dc5924405e103e1/core/server/server.go#L67-L70)), so on the UDP port a plain HTTP/3 client gets no reply at all. Without obfs, the same client gets the masquerade page. The TCP listeners are started separately and do not go through obfs ([server.go#L1644-L1660](https://github.com/apernet/hysteria/blob/ca8fbd874fd6ca82413948de6dc5924405e103e1/app/cmd/server.go#L1644-L1660)), so `listenHTTP`/`listenHTTPS` keep serving the masquerade site over TCP, though their responses still advertise `Alt-Svc: h3` on the obfuscated UDP port.
